title: Battus
source: P. Ovidius Naso, Metamorphoses, ed. Hugo Magnus (Gotha: F.A. Perthes), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-latinLit phi0959.phi006.perseus-lat2, sha256 fb3fdb1d8a4a3b82. Collated against The Latin Library (cltk mirror) as a disagreement detector only. Original spelling kept. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed Classical (restored) Latin, applied consistently. All translations were made fresh from the Latin for Lectorium.
about: The god of Delphi, whom Ovid turns aside to address directly, is not there when the son of Philyra weeps and begs for his help: he is away in Elis and Messenia in a shepherd's skin, a woodland staff in one hand and a seven-reed pipe in the other. While the pipe charms him the cattle stray unguarded into the fields of Pylos, and the son of Maia drives them off and hides them. One old man has seen it — Battus, who keeps the pastures and brood mares of rich Neleus — and is bought off with a single cow; then the thief changes shape, comes back, and doubles the price to have the same secret told. Watch how Ovid hands the old man's own words straight back reversed, and how the tale ends by taking the stone's side.

sentences.t:
Flebat opemque tuam frustra Philyreius heros,
Delphice, poscebat.
sentences.l: He was weeping, and your aid, in vain, the Philyrean hero — O Delphian — kept demanding.
sentences.i: He wept, and in vain the hero born of Philyra kept begging your help, O god of Delphi.
sentences.n: Apostrophe: Ovid breaks off from the story to address Apollo directly ('Delphice' is a vocative) and keeps him in the second person for the next several lines, so that the whole scene becomes an account of the god's absence. 'Philyreius heros' is Chiron, named by his mother Philyra where English would simply name the man. The two imperfects hold the moment open — he went on weeping, went on asking.

sentences.t:
Nam nec rescindere magni
iussa Iovis poteras, nec, si rescindere posses,
tunc aderas: Elin Messeniaque arva colebas.
sentences.l: For neither could you annul the commands of great Jupiter, nor, if you could annul them, were you then at hand: you were dwelling in Elis and the Messenian fields.
sentences.i: For you could not undo great Jupiter's decrees; and even if you could have undone them, you were not there at the time — you were living in Elis and the fields of Messenia.
sentences.n: A double excuse offered on the god's behalf: he had not the power, and in any case he was elsewhere. 'si rescindere posses' is an unreal protasis, but the apodosis stays in the plain indicative ('tunc aderas'), so the second reason is not hypothetical at all — it is simply a fact laid alongside. Elis and Messenia lie in the western Peloponnese; what he was doing there comes next.

sentences.t:
Illud erat tempus, quo te pastoria pellis
texit onusque fuit baculum silvestre sinistrae,
alterius dispar septenis fistula cannis.
sentences.l: That was the time in which a shepherd's hide covered you, and the burden of your left hand was a woodland staff, of the other an uneven pipe of seven reeds.
sentences.i: That was the season when a shepherd's skin clothed you, and your left hand's load was a stick cut in the woods, your right hand's a pipe of seven uneven reeds.
sentences.n: The god in herdsman's dress: 'pastoria pellis' is an animal skin worn as a cloak, and the verb 'texit' means it covered him as much as clothed him. In the second half the verb is not repeated — 'onus fuit' carries over, and 'sinistrae' and 'alterius' are both genitives, the left hand's burden and the other hand's. 'dispar ... septenis cannis' describes the panpipe itself, whose reeds are cut to differing lengths; 'dispar' is uneven, not unequal to anything.

sentences.t:
Dumque amor est curae, dum te tua fistula mulcet,
incustoditae Pylios memorantur in agros
processisse boves.
sentences.l: And while love is a care to you, while your own pipe soothes you, the cattle are recorded to have gone forward, unguarded, into the Pylian fields.
sentences.i: And while love was your concern and your own pipe was charming you, the cattle — so it is remembered — strayed untended into the fields of Pylos.
sentences.n: 'memorantur ... processisse' is the nominative with the infinitive after a verb of reporting: the subject stands in the nominative ('boves') and the reporting verb is passive, so the sentence says the cows are remembered to have gone, and Ovid quietly declines to vouch for it. 'boves' is held back past its own infinitive to the end of the sentence. The two 'dum' clauses place the blame exactly: the god was busy loving and busy playing, and 'incustoditae' is predicative — the cattle went because no one was watching them.

sentences.t:
Videt has Atlantide Maia
natus et arte sua silvis occultat abactas.
sentences.l: These the one born of Maia, daughter of Atlas, sees, and by his own art hides them, driven off, in the woods.
sentences.i: The son of Maia, Atlas' daughter, spies them, and with his own craft drives them away and hides them in the woods.
sentences.n: 'Atlantide Maia natus' is Mercury, named by his mother in an ablative of origin — born from Maia the daughter of Atlas — which is Ovid's habit throughout this tale: the thief is never once called by his name. 'abactas' packs a whole action into a participle, since he must drive the cattle off before he can hide them; English needs two verbs where Latin needs one word. 'arte sua' is his own particular art, and the art in question is theft.

sentences.t:
Senserat hoc furtum nemo nisi notus in illo
rure senex; Battum vicinia tota vocabant.
sentences.l: No one had noticed this theft except an old man well known in that countryside; Battus the whole neighbourhood used to call him.
sentences.i: No one had caught the theft but one old man, a familiar figure in that countryside; the whole neighbourhood called him Battus.
sentences.n: 'vicinia tota' is a singular collective taking a plural verb ('vocabant') — construction according to the sense, since a neighbourhood is people. The pluperfect 'senserat' places the noticing before the narrative present: the theft already had its witness while it was being committed.

sentences.t:
Divitis hic saltus herbosaque pascua Nelei
nobiliumque greges custos servabat equarum.
sentences.l: He, as guardian, used to watch the glades and grassy pastures of rich Neleus, and the herds of his noble mares.
sentences.n: 'custos' stands in apposition to the subject: watching was his office, which is what makes him a credible witness and his silence worth paying for. The genitive 'Nelei' governs all three objects — glades, pastures and herds alike belong to the king at Pylos. 'nobilium ... equarum' is pedigree rather than rank: brood mares of good stock.

sentences.l: Him he feared, and with a coaxing hand drew him aside, and to him "whoever you are, stranger," he says, "if by chance someone shall seek these herds, deny that you have seen them;"
sentences.i: This man he feared; so with a coaxing hand he drew him aside and said, "Whoever you are, friend, if anyone should come asking after this herd, deny you ever saw it."
sentences.n: Magnus prints 'timuit', he was afraid of him; other editions print 'tenuit', he took hold of him — the one makes the god nervous, the other merely brisk, and the coaxing hand suits either. 'hospes' names either party to the guest-bond, so it is at once 'stranger' and 'my friend', and the god is invoking a courtesy he is about to trade on. 'vidisse nega' negates the whole reported fact in the one verb, where English has to say that you did not see.

sentences.t:
neu gratia facto
nulla rependatur, nitidam cape praemia vaccam” —
et dedit. Accepta voces has reddidit hospes:
sentences.l: "and lest no thanks be repaid for the service, take, as your reward, this sleek cow" — and he gave it. The cow received, the stranger returned these words:
sentences.i: "and so that the favour should not go unthanked, take this sleek cow as your payment" — and he handed it over. Taking it, the stranger gave him back these words:
sentences.n: 'neu ... nulla rependatur' is a purpose clause with both negatives left standing — literally that no gratitude be not repaid — where English must drop one of them. 'praemia' is a neuter plural in apposition to a single cow, the plural of reward-in-general applied to one animal. 'Accepta' is an ablative absolute with its noun omitted: the cow, having been taken; Latin can leave out what the sentence has only just named.

sentences.t:
“Tutus eas: lapis iste prius tua furta loquetur”,
et lapidem ostendit. Simulat Iove natus abire,
mox redit, et versa pariter cum voce figura
sentences.l: "Safe may you go: that stone there will speak of your thefts sooner," and he pointed at the stone. Jove's son pretends to depart, soon returns, and, his shape changed together with his voice,
sentences.i: "Go safe: that stone will tell of your thefts before ever I do," and the old man pointed to it. The son of Jove makes a show of leaving, is presently back, his shape altered and his voice with it,
sentences.n: 'eas' is a wish in the subjunctive — may you go — with 'tutus' predicative: go, and be safe in the going. 'iste' is the stone being pointed at, the demonstrative of what stands near the person addressed. 'prius' leaves the comparison unspoken, sooner than I shall, and the reader is meant to supply it. Then 'versa ... figura' is an ablative absolute with 'pariter cum voce' folded inside it, so that two Latin words do the work of an English clause.

sentences.t:
“rustice, vidisti siquas hoc limite” dixit
“ire boves, fer opem furtoque silentia deme:
iuncta suo pariter dabitur ubi femina tauro.”
sentences.l: "Countryman, if you have seen any cows go along this track," he said, "bring help and take the silence away from the theft: whereupon a female shall be given, coupled likewise with her own bull."
sentences.i: "Fellow, if you have seen any cattle pass along this path," he said, "lend me help and strip this theft of its silence — and then a cow shall be yours, and her bull along with her."
sentences.n: The bribe is now two beasts where it was one, which is exactly what the next line's doubled reward depends on. 'furto silentia deme' is a dative of separation — take the silence off the theft — where English takes it from. Magnus's line is hard: 'ubi' has to be read as 'whereupon', and other editions print 'pretium tibi', a cow with her bull shall be given you as your price, which is the sense either way. 'rustice' is the disguised god's word for the man, half address and half sneer.

sentences.t:
At senior, postquam est merces geminata, “sub illis
montibus” inquit “erunt”: et erant sub montibus illis.
sentences.l: But the older man, after the payment had been doubled, "under those mountains," he says, "they will be": and they were under those mountains.
sentences.i: But the old man, once the price was doubled, said, "They will be under those mountains there" — and under those mountains they were.
sentences.n: The joke is in the grammar. Battus hedges with a future, they will be, as though he were guessing; Ovid answers with the flat imperfect indicative, and answers the word order too — 'sub illis montibus' comes straight back reversed as 'sub montibus illis'. The betrayal is complete inside a single line and the narrator adds no comment at all. 'senior' is the comparative used as plain description, the older man, not older than anyone in particular.

sentences.t:
Risit Atlantiades et “me mihi, perfide, prodis?
me mihi prodis?” ait, periuraque pectora vertit
in durum silicem, qui nunc quoque dicitur index,
inque nihil merito vetus est infamia saxo.
sentences.l: The son of Atlas' line laughed, and "me to myself, faithless one, do you betray? me to myself do you betray?" he says, and he turned the perjured breast into hard flint, which even now is called the Informer, and in the stone, which deserved none of it, the old ill-fame stands.
sentences.i: Atlas' grandson laughed and said, "Me — to me — you betray me, faithless? Me, to my own self?" and he turned that perjured breast to hard flint, which even now they call the Informer; and the stone, which never deserved it, carries the old disgrace still.
sentences.n: 'me mihi prodis' is the whole point of the tale and Ovid lets him say it twice: the god was buying silence about himself, from himself, at his own second price. 'quoque' here is the plain adverb inside 'nunc quoque', even now — worth checking each time, since the same letters elsewhere in this poem are 'quo-que', and by which. 'index' is the informer, the one who points a thing out, and the stone keeps it as a name. The last line turns the victim into the rock: 'nihil merito ... saxo', the stone earned none of this, and carries the reputation anyway.
